message.content:
Below is a concise overview of the key rights and protections you have as a tenant in Texas. (This is general information and not legal advice; for specific situations you may want to consult an attorney or a local tenant‑rights organization.) | Area | What the law says | Practical Tips | |------|-------------------|----------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlords may charge up to one month’s rent for a furnished unit and two months for an unfurnished unit.
• The deposit must be returned within 30 days after you move out, minus any lawful deductions (e.g., unpaid rent, damage beyond normal wear). | • Get a written receipt and keep a copy of the lease.
• Take photos of the unit before moving in and after moving out. | | **Habitability** | • Texas law requires landlords to maintain the premises in a safe, sanitary, and livable condition.
• Repairs for things like plumbing, heating, and structural issues must be made promptly. | • Report problems in writing (email or letter) and keep copies.
• If the landlord fails to fix major issues, you may withhold rent or pursue a repair‑and‑deduct claim. | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Late fees are allowed only if the lease states them and they are reasonable. | • Keep records of all payments (bank statements, receipts). | | **Entry Rights** | • Landlords must give at least 24 hours written notice before entering, except in emergencies.
• Entry is allowed for repairs, inspections, or showing the unit to prospective tenants or buyers. | • Ask for a written notice and keep a copy. | | **Discrimination** | • Under federal Fair Housing Act and Texas Property Code §92.001, landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, disability, or other protected classes. | • If you suspect discrimination, file a complaint with the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) or the Texas Commission on Human Rights. | | **Lease Termination** | • Either party can terminate a month‑to‑month lease with 30 days’ written notice.
• For fixed‑term leases, the landlord must provide a valid reason for early termination (e.g., non‑payment, violation of lease). | • Review your lease for any specific termination clauses. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlords must follow the Texas Property Code §92.001 and provide a written notice (e.g., 30‑day notice for non‑payment).
• Eviction must go through the court; landlords cannot forcibly remove you. | • Respond promptly to notices.
• If you receive an eviction notice, consider contacting a tenant‑rights group or attorney. | | **Repair‑and‑Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to repair a major issue, you may repair it yourself and deduct the cost from your rent, but you must follow the proper procedure (written notice, reasonable cost, etc.). | • Keep receipts and document the issue. | | **Privacy** | • Landlords cannot enter without notice, except in emergencies. | • Keep a log of any entries. | | **Utilities** | • The lease should specify who pays utilities. | • Verify utility responsibilities before signing. | | **Subletting** | • Subletting is allowed only if the lease permits it or the landlord consents. | • Get written permission if required. | | **Maintenance of Common Areas** | • Landlords must keep common areas clean and safe. | • Report any hazards (e.g., broken stair railings). | | **Legal Assistance** | • Texas has several tenant‑rights organizations (e.g., Texas Tenants Union, Texas Legal Services Center). | • Seek help if you face eviction or disputes. | ### Quick Checklist Before Signing a Lease 1. **Read the lease thoroughly** – look for clauses on rent, security deposit, maintenance responsibilities, entry notice, and termination. 2. **Ask for a written receipt** of any security deposit. 3. **Document the unit’s condition** with photos or a video walkthrough. 4. **Confirm utility responsibilities** and any service providers. 5. **Verify that the landlord is licensed** (if required) and that the property complies with local building codes. --- #### When Things Go Wrong | Issue | First Step | Next Step | |-------|------------|-----------| | Landlord refuses to make repairs | Write a formal notice (email/letter) and keep a copy | If no response in 10–14 days, consider filing a repair‑and‑deduct claim or contacting a local tenant‑rights group | | Unreasonable late fee | Review lease terms; if fee is not stated or is excessive, dispute in writing | If unresolved, seek mediation or small‑claims court | | Eviction notice | Respond promptly; request a hearing if you believe the eviction is unjust | Contact a lawyer or tenant‑rights organization for representation | --- #### Resources - **Texas Property Code** – the statutory framework for landlord‑tenant relations. - **Texas Commission on Human Rights** – for discrimination complaints. - **U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD)** – for federal fair housing issues. - **Texas Tenants Union** – advocacy and legal assistance. - **Local legal aid offices** – free or low‑cost legal help. --- **Bottom line:** As a Texas tenant, you have the right to a safe, habitable home, timely notice before entry, protection against discrimination, and a clear process for handling disputes. Keep thorough records, communicate in writing, and know where to turn for help if your landlord violates your rights.
